en: The Sūtra on Seeing the Correct, also titled the Sūtra on the Transformation of Consciousness in Birth and Death, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Tanwulan of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Jeta Grove Monastery. At that very time...
At the time of the meal, he led five hundred bhikṣus, as well as bodhisattvas and one thousand upāsakas, all carrying offerings, out of the city of Rājagṛha.

There was a great tree named Sweet Fragrance; its roots were deep and its trunk massive, its branches and leaves lush and flourishing, and its flowers and fruits were crimson. Its flavor was sweet and delicious, and beneath the tree was a broad, level area where stones had been gathered to form a seat.
The Buddha intended to rest there, so the upāsakas immediately spread out mats for seating.
The Buddha then sat down, and his disciples and bodhisattvas likewise took their seats.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Jiànzhèng who had newly donned the dharma robes. Doubts arose in his mind, and he thought to himself:
"The Buddha says there is rebirth in future lives; yet, once a person has died, there is no one who returns to report what happened. How can this be known?"
"You should ask the Buddha about this.
Before he had even spoken, the Buddha already knew it in advance.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke first:
“Disciples! This tree was originally planted from a single seed. Nourished by the four great elements, it has grown to such vast abundance that it covers all of you.

When it was originally a seed, its roots, trunk, leaves, and fruit did not yet exist and were not yet seen; only when it encountered the interconnected conditions of the four great elements did sprouts, leaves, stems, joints, flowers, and fruit arise. Increasing beyond its original state, it naturally became a tree, spreading its branches far and wide.”

At first it is called the seed; from the seed a sprout arises, from the sprout a stalk arises, from the stalk leaves arise, from the leaves flowers arise, and from the flowers fruit arises. Thus they undergo successive transformations and changes; they are not the same as before, yet they do not depart from what was before. Therefore, their names are not permanent names.
It eventually became a great tree; the tree produced fruit, and the fruit grew into trees again. As the years and months passed, they increased in this manner beyond measure.
The Buddha told his disciples:
“If one were to gather together the flowers, fruits, stems, nodes, roots, and trunks, could one make them return to the state of a seed?”
The disciples all said, "It cannot be obtained. That has already undergone transformation;

it cannot be restored. It gradually decays until the seed is produced again from the core. In this way, it is endless—transforming and changing as it is reborn, finally all returning to decay, such that it can never again be made into its original core."
The Buddha told his disciples: "Birth and death are also like this. Consciousness is the dharma that gives rise [to existence];

that which gives rise is ignorance (*moha*). Ignorance leads to craving and attachment. Ignorance is like the seed of that tree; though the seed is small, it grows into a great tree. A single instance of ignorance brings about many causes and conditions, and all these many causes and conditions originally emerge from ignorance."

From ignorance arise volitional formations; from volitional formations arises consciousness; from consciousness arise name-and-form; from name-and-form arise the six sense bases; from the six sense bases arises contact; from contact arises feeling; from feeling arises craving; from craving arises grasping; from grasping arises becoming; from becoming arises birth; and from birth arise old age and death.

When the twelve links of dependent origination combine to form a body, that body must inevitably face old age and death; the consciousness shifts and transforms, proceeding according to its past actions.

It encounters new parents, receives a new physical form, acquires new six sense-faculties, new habits, new experiences of suffering and pleasure, and new customs—all of which are not the former, and thus one cannot return to them again.

Because they no longer recognize what is familiar, they regard what they have newly seen as existing and as permanent; they become attached to what they rely upon, calling it the truth, and they claim there is no past life or future life.
The conscious spirit (*vijñāna*) migrates and transmigrates, existing in accordance with one's past actions.

Once the conscious spirit has migrated, one acquires new parents, receives a new body, undergoes new sensory experiences (*ṣaḍāyatana*), adopts new habits, encounters new suffering and pleasure, and enters into new customs; thus, one no longer recognizes the former state and cannot return to the old body, old habits, or old circumstances—just as a tree, once grown, can no longer revert to being a seed.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha had said, rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha:
"My mind has not yet eliminated nor resolved the essential point. I now wish to pose a question born of ignorance; may the Buddha, out of compassion for us, explain it for our sake."

Since my birth, I have seen many people die—whether fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, or various relatives; whether friends who cherished and loved one another, or enemies who harbored mutual hatred. Yet after death, their consciousness and spirit never once returned to face us to answer regarding their good or evil deeds.
Why is this? By what obstacles is the consciousness obstructed so that it cannot return to report face-to-face to people?
We pray that you will explain this for us in detail, so that our fetters may be severed and we may quickly attain the vision of the Truth.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"That consciousness is formless; as it undergoes transition, it exists in accordance with one's actions.
If the body performs meritorious deeds, the consciousness of merit is reborn accordingly, yet it cannot return face-to-face to repay the person."
Why is this? It is like a smith who melts stone to make iron; once it has become iron, he then casts it to form vessels. Once it has become a vessel, could it ever be made into stone again?
Jian Zheng said: "Truly it is not possible.
Once stone has turned into iron, it can never again become stone."
The Buddha said:
"The transmigration of consciousness abides in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), like stone that has been melted to become iron.

From the intermediate state, it transmigrates to receive another body, like iron that has been cast into a vessel; as its form dissolves and its substance changes, it cannot return to its former consciousness."
Why is this? Because the good and evil of one’s actions, consciousness goes forth to receive; it undergoes transformation and change, just as stone becomes iron.
By practicing the five virtues and receiving a human body, one then has parents once more.
Once parents have come together, there are six fetters of confinement:
first, dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), from which one cannot return;
second, entering within the womb according to the body one is to receive.
Third, at the moment of birth, one is oppressed by pain and forgets former consciousness and perceptions;
fourth, upon falling to the ground, former conscious recollections cease and new perceptions and views arise;
fifth, once born, one immediately becomes attached to food, and because of these greedy thoughts, conscious recollections are severed.
Sixth: from birth until one grows up, one practices what is newly seen; consciousness perishes and there is no longer any residual consciousness. "O disciples!

It is like a merchant who travels through the four quarters of the world and fully experiences both suffering and joy. He then directs his thoughts toward a single district or kingdom in the east; once this thought has arisen, the thoughts of the other three directions perish."

Birth and death are also like this: from this world one performs karmic actions and proceeds to receive them in a future life; once they have been received, new perceptions arise, and thus the consciousness and perceptions of the previous state cease, just as when a merchant focuses his thoughts on one direction, the perceptions of the other three directions cease.

By means of these six matters, one is bound, obscured, and obstructed, such that one no longer returns to the original consciousness; it is like a seed becoming a tree or stone becoming iron—the original is transformed and its name changed, so that it can no longer return to face its former self and provide a response.
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, it is like a potter who kneads clay to form a vessel; once it has been fired with fire and transformed into a jar, how could that jar ever be made to return to being clay again?"
The disciples all said, “It truly cannot be done.
The clay has already been fired and transformed into tiles; it cannot be made to return to being clay again.”
The Buddha said:
"Disciples! The consciousness transmigrates and, according to its karma, receives a body, just as clay is formed into a tile."
When a person lacks the practice of the Way, they no longer recognize their former selves; thus, they cannot return to respond to one another. Bhikṣus!
It is further like a tree several tens of spans in girth, which a skilled craftsman then carves and engraves with hundreds of kinds of exquisite and ingenious designs.
"If a person wished to gather together the wood shavings and sawdust from a carved object and, through skillful means, restore it to become a tree again,
would that be possible? The disciples replied, "Truly, it would not."

"The tree has already been cut down and split apart; it has been carved into pieces until exhausted. Its branches and leaves are withered and decayed, and can no longer be gathered back together to form a tree.
The Buddha said to his disciples:

"When the consciousness-spirit (vijñāna) performs good or evil deeds in this world, at the point of death the consciousness migrates. It receives a body according to its karma. What is seen and what is practiced is no longer the former body; it cannot be returned to, nor can it recognize the old face to answer or repay [the past]."
"Just as when a tree has been cut down, it cannot be gathered back together to grow again," the Buddha said, "Furthermore,
it is like a master craftsman who burns sand to make red glass, which is then further transformed into a white shape and changed into something like water."
"If the disciples wish to cause this red [substance] to return to being sand again,
can it be accomplished? The disciples replied, "Truly, it cannot."
"Once sand has been burned and transformed, it cannot be restored to its original state.
The Buddha said,
"Birth and death are also like this."

When a person has not yet developed the aspiration for the Way and lacks the pure eye, at the death of the body the consciousness departs; it undergoes transformation according to its past actions, transmigrating into another form. As it passes through different lifetimes and repeatedly enters a womb, its perceptions and habits all become distinct; because it no longer recognizes its former self, it is like sand turned into red dye that can never return to its original state.
The Buddha said: "Disciples! Furthermore, it is like water:

when placed in a round vessel, its form becomes round; when moved to a square container, its form becomes square; whether large, small, curved, or straight, it conforms to whatever place it falls into."

"O disciples! Birth and death are likewise thus: the consciousness-spirit is fundamentally non-existent and possesses no permanent form; according to the good or evil deeds one performs, it immediately proceeds to receive a body."
Whether white or black, long or short, suffering or pleasure, good or evil—these transformations and experiences follow one’s conduct like water taking the shape of its vessel.

Or, having committed unrighteous acts while among humans, one dies and falls into the realm of animals, receiving an evil body; because one no longer recognizes [one's former self], one cannot answer face-to-face.

"Disciples! It is like the cicada-insect (*chuchü*), which is born from within the earth; having neither sound nor wings, it undergoes transformation upon meeting the conditions of the season and becomes a cicada. It flies up to perch upon trees, its chirping never ceasing."
The Buddha asked his disciples,
"Would it be possible to cause a cicada to return to the earth and become a chrysalis?
The disciples replied:
"Truly, it is impossible.

Once the cicada larvae have transformed, having left the yin and entered the yang, their physical forms have changed and become different; they are destined for death each day, perhaps to be devoured by various birds, and cannot return to being cicada larvae."
The Buddha said:
"Disciples, birth and death are also like this."

When life ends and the body dies, consciousness transmigrates and receives a new body; obscured by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), their perceptions and habits differ, and they likewise undergo old age and death there, unable to return again. Because they no longer recognize one another, they cannot provide answers face-to-face.
"It is like a cicada on a tree; it can never again become a cicada larva.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"Furthermore, it is like a piece of raw meat; if it is not eaten after its time has passed, it will rot and breed maggots. Would one be able to make it become fresh meat again?"
The disciples said, "Truly it cannot be done;
the meat is already putrid and rotten, and it is impossible to make it fresh and clean again."
The Buddha said:
"Birth and death are also like this.

When a person dwells in the world, if their mind conceives evil, their speech utters evil, and their body performs evil, then at death their consciousness transmigrates and falls into a body in hell, or a body as an animal, or a body as a fish or insect. In whatever place they are reborn, they see things differently and are no longer the same as before; obscured by the net of their own transgressions, they no longer recognize their former selves and cannot return to face one another to give an account. It is just as that putrid meat cannot be made fresh and clean again."
The Buddha told his disciples:

"Furthermore, it is like a dark night on the last day of the month when the moon has set; suppose one were to place objects of five colors in the darkness and command a thousand or ten thousand people to look at those colored objects in the night. Would there be even a single person among them who could distinguish their blue, yellow, red, or white?"
The disciples all said:

"Even if there were hundreds of millions of people, or even an incalculable number of people, and they were made to observe it at night, none would ever see it; how then could one distinguish its five colors?"
The Buddha said:
"If someone were to hold up a torch to illuminate it and have people look at it, would it be possible for them to see it?
The disciples replied:
"A person relying on the light of a torch can distinguish all five colors.
The Buddha said, "If a foolish person turns his back on the torch and enters into the darkness, traveling to an extreme distance, could he hope to see the five colors? Could he possibly see them?"
The disciples said, “This fool turns his back on light and moves toward darkness; as he progresses further into obscurity, there will never be a time when he sees forms.
The Buddha told the disciples:
"Human beings in the cycle of birth and death are also like this.

All people—including those that crawl, fly, or wriggle—having already received a physical form, are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance and lack the practice of the Path. They do not study the affairs of the body or the mind; they have not yet attained the eye of wisdom, yet they wish to know the destination of birth and death and the coming and going of the *vijñāna* (consciousness). To try to answer such things face-to-face is like trying to see the five colors on a night of the new moon when it is dark and overcast; one will ultimately be unable to see them."

If one practices the sūtras and precepts, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and maintains control over the mind, thereby proceeding toward pure conduct, it is like following a person holding a torch and clearly seeing the five colors.

If a person follows the teachings of the Buddha, they will be able to discern death and birth, clearly seeing the five realms of existence and the places where the consciousness-spirit falls—whether good or evil—just as a torch illuminates forms, perceiving them all with complete clarity.

If a person from the outset does not study the matters of body and mind, but turns their back on the sutras and precepts, following the three worldly currents of common custom, indulging in their own whims, and severing the true Dharma—neither believing nor delighting in it, and refusing to practice it—they are like one who turns their back on a torch and enters the darkness; their knots of doubt grow ever more severe, and they will never reach a time of insight, realization, or understanding.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"Do not follow your own foolish, obstructed, and fettered inclinations by failing to believe in the pure, true, and correct Way; do not cause yourselves to fall into hell and suffer physical pain."
"I have therefore cited this analogy so that you may understand it clearly.
You all should always diligently practice the sutras and precepts, keeping them firmly in your hearts.
The Buddha addressed his disciples:

"Human life consists of the physical form received from the world; what is seen with the fleshly eye is the present reality, clearly and distinctly perceived by parents and relatives, yet one cannot again see or know the place from which one came in a previous life."

Thereupon, when one undergoes old age and death and is reborn in a future life to receive another physical form, one will likewise be unable to recognize the affairs of this present life. Why is this so?

In one life and one death, the consciousness-spirit undergoes transformation; among the twelve links of dependent origination, ignorance is its master, for it revolves in a state of dull stupor and profound darkness, failing to recognize itself.

“Disciples! It is like boiling and refining white silk and dyeing it various colors—blue, yellow, red, or black. Because its original nature has been transformed and altered, it can never be returned to its former state.”

The transformation of birth and death is like silk taking on dye; consciousness has no permanent substance, yet it becomes defiled through its attachments according to its conduct. Lacking the pure eye of wisdom, one does not recognize the cause; the mind takes phenomena as its basis, and whatever it conceives immediately comes to fruition.

In a single lifetime, a person’s mental thoughts are manifold; they receive retribution for good and evil, receiving the new while the old ceases. Such is the law of birth and death, the constant nature of deluded darkness.

If one wishes to know and see the coming and going of birth and death, one should extensively study and practice the affairs of body and mind, enter deeply into purity, and contemplate from beginning to end; only then will one awaken, like rising from sleep.
The Buddha told his disciples:

"The consciousness-spirit (vijñāna) is a phenomenon of delusion and darkness; it produces good and evil deeds during life, and at death it transmigrates to receive its retribution. It manifests signs according to those good and evil deeds, just as fire depends on fuel: when the fuel is exhausted, the fire is extinguished."
If the mental consciousness does not perform good or evil deeds, it likewise ceases and there is nothing seen.
Those who have not attained the Way sink and drift in birth and death, revolving without awareness.
It is like a defiled mirror, obscured and stained by grime; when held up to one's face, nothing at all can be seen.

When the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is turbid and obscured, as it wanders through the cycle of birth and death, it becomes filled with the darkness of dread and fear, and being dragged along by calamity and fortune, it no longer recognizes its original nature—just like a mirror fouled by filth.
"Furthermore, it is like deep, turbid water: although fish and insects are present within it, they cannot be seen at all;
likewise, when birth and death are in chaos and the mind is obscured by the hindrances of grief and anxiety, one forgets the past as one is reborn, just like that turbid water."
It is like walking with one's eyes closed in the darkness of night, seeing nothing at all.

The obscurity of birth and death causes one to flow along according to calamity or fortune; whether experiencing joy or distress, one is bound by what is received and no longer recognizes [the truth], just like one who walks with eyes closed at night.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"Now that I have become a Buddha, my eye of wisdom is pure; all births and deaths, and the coming and going within the three realms, the Buddha fully knows and sees."
For example, when crystal, lapis lazuli, or precious gems are strung together with colored threads, both blue and yellow are clearly visible;
the Buddha views birth and death as one observes these strung beads.
For example, just as in clear, limpid water where the bottom is visible and the fish and insects within it are all seen nakedly,
so does the Buddha view birth and death, like fish in clear water.
"Just as a great bridge is never without the constant flow of people passing back and forth,
so does the Buddha view those in birth and death who travel through the five realms of existence, as one observes the people crossing a bridge."
"Just as a high mountain can be seen clearly from afar, the Buddha’s mind is lofty and far-reaching;
he fully knows the cycle of birth and death, with nothing that he does not discern.
The Buddha told his disciples:
“You should follow my instruction, and you shall come to fully know the events of a thousand billion kalpas of birth and death.

You must practice the essential path of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path—to remove the defilements of the mind, extinguish the three poisons, and dissolve the knots of doubt. Thereupon, you will behold purity, attain the wisdom-mind of a Buddha, and know the affairs of the past and future as clearly as looking into a bright mirror, seeing everything without exception.”
The Buddha told his disciples:
"Whatever good or evil deeds people perform in this world, they will all receive their corresponding retribution in the world after death.

However, because people have not yet attained the three kinds of pure eyes, they do not see or know it; they no longer recognize its origin, being bound by the six attachments and veiled by obscurations. Because they act with only the physical eye, they do not perceive the basis of this reciprocal retribution and thus claim that it does not exist."

Those who have not yet attained the Way all engage in turbid and defiled conduct; how much more so those submerged in ignorance, who transmigrate through birth and death, repeatedly receiving physical forms? Their physical eyes are dazzled and deluded; they abandon the old and bind themselves to the new, their fourfold sufferings agitating them in turmoil, such that they ultimately cannot attain knowledge to respond to and report upon the nature of their own conduct.

"Those among the people of the present age who either receive blessings or suffer calamities, or who feel mutual affection or harbor mutual hatred—these are the evidences of the retributive responses for their past deeds."
Because they lack the three pure eyes, they neither see nor know, and thus remain bound by doubt.

Since the beginning of all beings’ births in this world, they have been accompanied by ignorance; lacking the pure conduct of the Path, they yet desire to know the events of past lives and recognize the effects of karmic retribution. This is like one who wishes to write without hands or to see without eyes—it can never be accomplished.
Therefore, when a Buddha appears in the world, he expounds and manifests the Way of the sutras to enlighten the minds of men.

Those who wish to know and perceive the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*) as it wanders through birth and death and undergoes its retributions should follow the Buddha's teachings and practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). By restraining and commanding the mind, by harmonizing and rectifying the mind, and by entering the subtlety of dhyāna and samādhi, one may then fully understand the matters of where the consciousness-spirit falls and its coming and going.

“O you disciples! You should diligently study and understand the affairs of the body and the affairs of the mind; fully comprehend all opposing conditions and, upon their arrival, eliminate them so as not to be confused or misled, remaining steadfast in the True Dharma.”
"Do not cease in this way; that which you have questioned can now be understood.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"The conscious spirit (vijñāna) has a name but no form; it follows good and evil deeds and takes the four great elements as its substance."

At birth, the body is small, the sense faculties are not yet complete, and consciousness and vision are likewise limited; what is known is incomplete. As one grows up, the six sense organs become fully developed, and consciousness follows along with the physical form. The various habits of craving and desire increase daily until they reach full maturity. Upon reaching old age, the four elements of the body become frail and emaciated, and consciousness likewise loses its clarity while the six sense organs decline.
Dwelling in this present life, one undergoes change and impermanence, no longer remaining as one was;
what was practiced and seen in youth is forgotten by old age—
how much more so when transitioning to another world, bound and obscured within the womb?

"Those who have not yet attained the aspiration for the Way, whose conduct is deluded and defiled by confusion, cannot perceive the coming and going of the mental consciousness or its reciprocal responses.

For a person who lacks the practice of the Way to hope to see and know the matters of past lives is like threading a needle in the dark of night or seeking fire within water; it can never be achieved."
"You, my disciples! You should diligently practice the sutras and the precepts, and reflect deeply upon where birth and death originally come from and where they ultimately return."
For what reason do they come and go?
What is their object of focus?
By contemplating with truth and precision the phenomena that are empty and non-existent, one attains purity, eliminates fetters, and the doubts within oneself are naturally resolved.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, he saw that the five hundred people of Right Practice and all the upāsakas had all attained the stage of srotāpanna;
and all the bodhisattvas had attained the samādhi of non-retrogression.

Each rose and circumambulated the Buddha three times; they prostrated with their heads touching the ground, and having completed their salutations, they all returned to the vihāra together with the Buddha.
This Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Seeing the Right is also titled the Sūtra on the Transformation of Consciousness in Birth and Death.
